questions.stem: A 42-year-old man was evaluated for a new pleural effusion. He had recently returned from a 2-year residence in Honduras. He described left-sided pleuritic chest pain and a nonproductive cough with a low-grade fever. His medical history was not remarkable. Investigations: CXR: moderate-sized left pleural effusion A thoracentesis was performed
questions.lead_in: What pleural fluid investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adenosine deaminase measurement The patient presents with a new pleural effusion after returning from an endemic area for tuberculosis. The concern is for a tuberculous effusion and an LDH, pH, or Gram stain would not help diagnose tuberculosis. An AFB stain would be low yield, and therefore the correct answer is an adenosine deaminase. An adenosine deaminase would be expected to be high in the setting of a tuberculous effusion, and of the choices listed would be the most helpful for establishing the diagnosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q12

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of fever, malaise, diarrhea, cough, and wheezing. He had returned 4 weeks earlier from a 3-week trip to Malawi. Prior to the trip he received HAV , typhoid, and Tdap vaccinations. He did not take malaria prophylaxis because he was concerned about possible side effects. During his trip he visited orphanages, participated in traditional baptism ceremonies in Lake Malawi, ate with locals, and visited a small hospital where he had contact with inpatients and outpatients. On examination his temperature was 38.2°C, and he had a widespread urticarial rash.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Schistosomiasis Based on the incubation period and symptoms, the most likely diagnosis of the options provided is acute schistosomiasis. Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) is a hypersensitivity response to the start of egg production by the adult worms and manifests with a variety of symptoms, including fever, dry cough, diarrhea, urticaria, and angioedema. Measles, dengue, and Marburg (one of the hemorrhagic fevers) would not present this late. Malaria is not associated with a rash. (Image from James WD, Elston DM, McMahon PJ. Parasitic infestations, stings, and bites. In Andrews’ Diseases of the Skin Clinical Atlas. Elsevier; 2018.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q43

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presented with fever, pleuritic chest pain, and diarrhea. She had also noted recurrent but transient urticaria during this time. She had traveled with her family to Costa Rica 4 weeks earlier where she had eaten local food, which included raw shellfish. A diagnosis of paragonimiasis was confirmed by serology.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Praziquantel While both praziquantel and bithionol have activity against paragonimiasis, praziquantel is a better tolerated agent and therefore the more appropriate first-line therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q9

questions.stem: A 45-year old woman was investigated for suspected Schistosoma infection. Limited clinical information was provided of abdominal discomfort and intermittent diarrhea. There was no epidemiologic history available to the laboratory regarding country of origin, travel, etc. Stool microscopy for ova, cysts, and parasites:
questions.lead_in: What schistosome species is responsible for her symptoms?
questions.explanation: S. mansoni There is a clear lateral spine present on diagnostic faecal sample, consistent with a diagnosis of S. mansoni. (Image from McPherson RA, Pincus MR. Henry’s Clinical Diagnosis and Management by Laboratory Methods . 23rd ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q21

questions.question: Q26 (2013 PM). From Caribbean, repeat GNB bacteremia.

parts.text: B) 3 steps in the pathogenesis of the causative organism?
C) What testing will confirm your diagnosis?

cohort_answer.text:
Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection syndrome
Filariform larvae in soil penetrate human skin and migrate to small intestine; Larvae migrate via bloodstream and lymphatics to lungs where they are eventually coughed and swallowed; In the small intestine, they become female adult worms that produce eggs in the intestinal mucosa that become rhabditiform larvae; Rhabditiform larvae in the gut become infective filariform larvae that can penetrate either the intestinal mucosa or the skin of the perianal area, resulting in autoinfection.
Concentrated stool examination for microscopy (larvae/eggs)
Hyperinfection: ivermectin x 7 days; Disseminated: Ivermectin + albendazole daily until stool/ sputum is neg x 2 weeks; Reduce immunosuppression

questions.question: [image-based question: bladder biopsy on PAS stain]

parts.text: What are 2 chronic infections associated with this organism?

questions.question: Nematode, cestode, trematode? and treatment
questions.model_answer:
Trichuris trichiura - nematode; treatment: albendazole 400 mg daily for 3 days (or mebendazole 500 mg x3 days), sometimes combined with ivermectin for heavy infection.
Strongyloides stercoralis - nematode; treatment: ivermectin 200 mcg/kg/day for 2 days.
Diphyllobothrium latum - cestode; treatment: praziquantel (single dose).
Schistosoma species - trematode; treatment: praziquantel.
Fasciola hepatica - trematode; treatment: triclabendazole (praziquantel is NOT effective against Fasciola).

questions.question: ADULT section. Name parasitic organism associated with the stem (genus and species).

parts.text: 50 year old from Taiwan with recurrent cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma
37 year old from Tanzania with portal hypertension
36 year old from Ethiopia with interstitial keratitis poor vision
38 year old from Mozambique with fibrosis in the bladder

questions.model_answer:
a) 50-year-old from Taiwan with recurrent cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma: Clonorchis sinensis.
b) 37-year-old from Tanzania with portal hypertension: Schistosoma mansoni (hepatosplenic schistosomiasis).
c) 36-year-old from Ethiopia with interstitial keratitis and poor vision: Onchocerca volvulus (river blindness).
d) 38-year-old from Mozambique with bladder wall fibrosis: Schistosoma haematobium.
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 3453-3461 (Schistosoma/Clonorchis); Onchocerca is outside this trematode chapter

questions.question: Complete the table: Organism | Nematode, Cestode, or Trematode | 1st Line Treatment, for Strongyloides, Fasciola, Schistosomiasis, Trichuris, Dibothriocephalus latum

parts.text: Complete table for Strongyloides, Fasciola, Schistosomiasis, Trichuris, Dibothriocephalus latum

cohort_answer.text: Strongyloides - Nematode - Ivermectin. Fasciola - Trematode - Triclabendazole. Schistosomiasis - Trematode - Praziquantel. Trichuris - Nematode - Albendazole. Dibothriocephalus latus - Cestode - Praziquantel. Rule: all nematodes use albendazole except Strongyloides (Ivermectin); all cestodes/trematodes use praziquantel except Fasciola (Triclabendazole).

Recurrent cholangitis and fibrosis: Clonorchis sinensis; Opisthorchis viverrini/felineus; Fasciola hepatica; Ascaris lumbricoides. Sclerosing keratitis: Acanthamoeba; Onchocerciasis.

questions.question: Patient recently immigrated from Ethiopia. Severe asthma not responding to standard treatment with inhaled beta agonists and inhaled corticosteroids oral corticosteroids. Noted to have eosinophilia. Develops hemoptysis

parts.text: What are 3 tests to help you make the diagnosis and what are you sampling?
What are 2 treatments for this patient?

cohort_answer.text: A) Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (response to Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi); causes dyspnea, cough, wheezing (esp night), chest discomfort, weight loss, malaise; commonly misdiagnosed as asthma; high eosinophils, high IgE, antifilarial antibodies; diffuse miliary lesions on CXR, patchy consolidation, cavitation, reticulonodular infiltrates, can lead to progressive fibrosis. Dx: microfilariae in lung/liver/lymph node bx. B) Nocturnal blood smear; anti-filarial antibodies; biopsy of lung/liver/lymph node for microfilaria; sputum for eosinophils; IgE and eosinophilia. C) DEC, Doxycycline, Ivermectin, Albendazole.

questions.question: Name the parasite that is associated with various long term effects

parts.text: Cholangiocarcinoma and recurrent cholangitis from taiwan

questions.model_answer: Cholangiocarcinoma/recurrent cholangitis from Taiwan: Clonorchis sinensis. Portal hypertension from sub-Saharan Africa: Schistosoma mansoni. Keratitis and blindness from Ethiopia: Onchocerca volvulus. Bladder wall fibrosis from sub-Saharan Africa: Schistosoma haematobium.

questions.question: Would corticosteroids be indicated in the following conditions:

parts.text: Neurocysticercosis with viable parenchymal cysts and no evidence of intracranial hypertension
Hydatid cyst at high risk of rupture and spillage

questions.model_answer:
a) TB meningitis: Yes - corticosteroids (dexamethasone) indicated, shown to reduce mortality.
b) Neurocysticercosis with viable parenchymal cysts, no intracranial hypertension: Yes - corticosteroids indicated (typically given with antihelminthic therapy to blunt the inflammatory response to dying cysts).
c) Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome): Yes - corticosteroids can be used for severe acute/hypersensitivity symptoms (Katayama fever), often together with or before antihelminthic therapy.
d) Hydatid cyst at high risk of rupture/spillage: No - corticosteroids are not routinely indicated; concern is instead for anaphylaxis/dissemination from spillage, managed with careful surgical/PAIR technique and perioperative albendazole, not steroids (steroids are not a standard preventive measure here).
questions.beyond_mandell: Reflects standard ID teaching on steroid indications in these conditions; specific figures not verified against this Mandell chapter (TB-only pagefile).

questions.question: Woman from Sudan immigrated. Screening revealed hematuria. She had an o/p which showed the following.

parts.text: what is the organism to the species level?
what is the long-term complication if not treated?

questions.model_answer:
a) Organism (to species level): Schistosoma haematobium (terminal-spined ova, hematuria, Sudan endemic).
b) Preferred treatment: praziquantel 40 mg/kg/day, given as two divided doses in a single day.
c) Long-term complication if untreated: chronic bladder fibrosis/calcification with obstructive uropathy and hydronephrosis, and increased risk of bladder squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.question: Q85 2023 Day 2. Woman from an African country, do not recall which, with painless hematuria, shows picture of schistosoma haematobium.

parts.text: What are patients at risk of in long term if not treated

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Schistosoma haematobium. Treatment of choice: Praziquantel 40 mg/kg/day in 1-2 doses x1 day. Long-term risks if untreated: Infertility; Ectopic pregnancy; Dysuria, UTI leading to bladder wall fibrosis/calcification, ureteral strictures, hydronephrosis, polyps, tumors, bladder neck obstruction, hydroureter, hydronephrosis leading to renal failure; increased risk of bladder cancer; ovarian granulomas.

questions.question: Q6 (2007). Woman returning from beach vacation. You are shown a poor quality picture of lesions on her abdomen, with multiple excoriations.

cohort_answer.text: A) Cutaneous larva migrans. B) Ancylostoma Brasiliense/caninum. C) Clinical diagnosis based on history and appearance of rash; emerging dermoscopy reports; fecal microscopy if GI symptoms for hookworm eggs. D) Dogs/cats excrete eggs into soil; eggs hatch to release rhabditiform larva; rhabditiform larva mature into filariform larva after 5-10 days becoming infective; filariform larva in soil penetrate human skin and produce inflammatory reaction along cutaneous migration route. E) Strongyloides (causes 'Larva Currens', more rapid); Gnathostoma (larva causes local swelling - edema/pain/pruritis/erythema). F) Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg PO x1-2 days.

questions.question: Q29 (2010 PM). Patient recently immigrated who has eosinophilia, but stool O+P negative. No real symptoms otherwise. Positive serology for Strongyloides and Schistosomiasis. Stool O+P negative

parts.text: A) Give 3 most common causes for asymptomatic eosinophilia in this patient
B) Give 2 reasons why the stool O+P is negative

cohort_answer.text: A) Strongyloides, Schistosomiasis, and hookworm are most commonly identified parasites (network +REDIVI data: S. stercoralis 34.4%, Schistosoma sp 11.0%, hookworm 8.6%). Other infectious causes: Filariae, HIV-1, various helminths. Non-infectious: allergy/atopic disease, drug reaction, hypoadrenalism, tumor-associated, hypereosinophilic syndromes. B) Stool O+P is very insensitive for Strongyloides (intermittent shedding) and Schistosomiasis; parasite not always excreted in stool (S. haematobium eggs excreted in urine not stool); for strongyloides eggs degrade before leaving body, need to look for rhabditiform larvae specifically; interval from acquisition to positive test result can be 3-4 weeks before GI symptoms/worms in intestine.

questions.question: For each of the following, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): TB meningitis; Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst; Cerebral malaria; Acute schistosomiasis; Large echinococcal cyst with risk of rupture during PAIR.

parts.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario and rationale

cohort_answer.text: Katayama fever (acute schisto) - yes (5 days pred 40mg followed by praziquantel per Mandell's). Neurocysticercosis intraventricular lesions not calcified and no hydrocephalus - yes (dexamethasone 6-8mg/day divided TID for 28 days, then slow taper over 2-8 weeks; not indicated in calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema; steroids lower praziquantel levels and increase albendazole levels, partial reason for albendazole use in limited CNS disease). TB meningitis - yes (non-HIV TB pericarditis can also use steroids, not for pleural; if HIV+ insufficient evidence). Ruptured echinococcus - no (not addressed in guidelines or UpToDate). Cerebral malaria - no

questions.question: Identify the parasite in the following scenarios: Patient from Taiwan with recurrent cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma.

parts.text: Identify the parasite: Patient from Taiwan with recurrent cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma.

cohort_answer.text: Clonorchis sinensis (Chinese Liver Fluke). Trematode (flat worm). Endemic to East Asia (Korea, China, Taiwan, Northern Vietnam). Typically infects humans from eating undercooked fish containing metacercariae. Treatment: Praziquantel 25mg/kg TID x1-2 days or Albendazole 10mg/kg/day x7 days (requires SAP).

questions.question: Identify the parasite in the following scenarios: Patient from Tanzania with portal hypertension.

parts.text: Identify the parasite: Patient from Tanzania with portal hypertension.

cohort_answer.text: Schistosoma mansoni. Trematode (flat-worm) blood fluke. Typically found in sub-Saharan Africa, Brazil, parts of North Africa (e.g. Egypt), Middle East. Infects humans from fresh water exposure where the snail intermediate host is present. Treatment: Praziquantel.

questions.question: Identify the parasite in the following scenarios: Patient from Zimbabwe with bladder fibrosis.

parts.text: Identify the parasite: Patient from Zimbabwe with bladder fibrosis.

cohort_answer.text: Schistosoma haematobium. Trematode (flat-worm) blood fluke. Typically found in sub-Saharan Africa, North Africa, Middle East. Infects humans from fresh water exposure where the snail intermediate host is present. Treatment: Praziquantel.

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Schistosoma haematobium. Treatment of choice: Praziquantel 40 mg/kg/day in 1-2 doses x1 day.

questions.question: Which malignancies are associated with the following organisms:
questions.model_answer:
Hepatitis C virus - hepatocellular carcinoma (and B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma).
HPV - cervical, anal, vulvar/vaginal/penile, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.
Schistosoma haematobium - bladder (squamous cell) carcinoma.
Clonorchis (sinensis) - cholangiocarcinoma.
H. pylori - gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric MALT lymphoma.
HHV-8 - Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease.
